L10@P1: Lattice-based cryptography is the use of conjectured hard problems on point lattices in R
L11@P1: n
L12@P1: as the foundation
L13@P1: for secure cryptographic systems. Attractive features of lattice cryptography include apparent resistance
L14@P1: to quantum attacks (in contrast with most number-theoretic cryptography), high asymptotic efficiency
L15@P1: and parallelism, security under worst-case intractability assumptions, and solutions to long-standing open
L16@P1: problems in cryptography.
L17@P1: This work surveys most of the major developments in lattice cryptography over the past ten years. The
L18@P1: main focus is on the foundational short integer solution (SIS) and learning with errors (LWE) problems (and
L19@P1: their more efficient ring-based variants), their provable hardness assuming the worst-case intractability of
L20@P1-2: standard lattice problems, and their many cryptographic applications.Contents

L95@P3-4: 2Chapter 1
L96@P4: Introduction
L97@P4: This survey provides an overview of lattice-based cryptography, the use of apparently hard problems on
L98@P4: point lattices in R
L99@P4: n
L100@P4: as the foundation for secure cryptographic constructions. Lattice cryptography has many
L101@P4: attractive features, some of which we now describe.
L102@P4: Conjectured security against quantum attacks. Most number-theoretic cryptography, such as the DiffieHellman protocol [DH76] and RSA cryptosystem [RSA78], relies on the conjectured hardness of integer
L103@P4: factorization or the discrete logarithm problem in certain groups. However, Shor [Sho97] gave efficient
L104@P4: quantum algorithms for all these problems, which would render number-theoretic systems insecure in a future
L105@P4: where large-scale quantum computers are available. By contrast, no efficient quantum algorithms are known
L106@P4: for the problems typically used in lattice cryptography; indeed, generic (and relatively modest) quantum
L107@P4: speedups provide the only known advantage over non-quantum algorithms.
L108@P4: Algorithmic simplicity, efficiency, and parallelism. Lattice-based cryptosystems are often algorithmically simple and highly parallelizable, consisting mainly of linear operations on vectors and matrices modulo
L109@P4: relatively small integers. Moreover, constructions based on “algebraic” lattices over certain rings (e.g., the
L110@P4: NTRU cryptosystem [HPS98]) can be especially efficient, and in some cases even outperform more traditional
L111@P4: systems by a significant margin.
L112@P4: Strong security guarantees from worst-case hardness. Cryptography inherently requires average-case
L113@P4: intractability, i.e., problems for which random instances (drawn from a specified probability distribution)
L114@P4: are hard to solve. This is qualitatively different from the worst-case notion of hardness usually considered
L115@P4: in the theory of algorithms and NP-completeness, where a problem is considered hard if there merely exist
L116@P4: some intractable instances. Problems that appear hard in the worst case often turn out to be easier on the
L117@P4: average, especially for distributions that produce instances having some extra “structure,” e.g., the existence
L118@P4: of a secret key for decryption.
L119@P4: In a seminal work, Ajtai [Ajt96] gave a remarkable connection between the worst case and the average
L120@P4: case for lattices: he proved that certain problems are hard on the average (for cryptographically useful
L121@P4: distributions), as long as some related lattice problems are hard in the worst case. Using results of this kind,
L122@P4: one can design cryptographic constructions and prove that they are infeasible to break, unless all instances of
L123@P4: certain lattice problems are easy to solve.1
L124@P4: 1Note that many number-theoretic problems used in cryptography, such as discrete logarithm and quadratic residuosity, also admit
L125@P4-5: 3Constructions of versatile and powerful cryptographic objects. Historically, cryptography was mainly
L126@P5: about sending secret messages. Yet over the past few decades, the field has blossomed into a discipline
L127@P5: having much broader and richer goals, encompassing almost any scenario involving communication or
L128@P5: computation in the presence of potentially malicious behavior. For example, the powerful notion of fully
L129@P5: homomorphic encryption (FHE), first envisioned by Rivest et al. [RAD78], allows an untrusted worker to
L130@P5: perform arbitrary computations on encrypted data, without learning anything about that data. For three decades
L131@P5: FHE remained an elusive “holy grail” goal, until Gentry [Gen09b, Gen09a] proposed the first candidate
L132@P5: construction of FHE, which was based on lattices (as were all subsequent constructions). More recently,
L133@P5: lattices have provided the only known realizations of other versatile and powerful cryptographic notions, such
L134@P5: as attribute-based encryption for arbitrary access policies [GVW13, BGG+14] and general-purpose code
L135@P5: obfuscation [GGH+13b].
L136@P5: 1.1 Scope and Organization
L137@P5: This work surveys most of the major developments in lattice cryptography over the past decade (since
L138@P5: around 2005). The main focus is on two foundational average-case problems, called the short integer
L139@P5: solution (SIS) and learning with errors (LWE) problems; their provable hardness assuming the worst-case
L140@P5: intractability of lattice problems; and the plethora of cryptographic constructions that they enable.
L141@P5: Most of this survey should be generally accessible to early-stage graduate students in theoretical computer
L142@P5: science, or even to advanced undergraduates. However, understanding the finer details of the cryptographic
L143@P5: constructions—especially the outlines of their security proofs, which we have deliberately left informal so
L144@P5: as to highlight the main ideas—may require familiarity with basic cryptographic definitions and paradigms,
L145@P5: which can be obtained from any graduate-level course or the textbooks by, e.g., Katz and Lindell [KL14] or
L146@P5: Goldreich [Gol01]. The reader who lacks such background is encouraged to focus on the essential ideas and
L147@P5: mechanics of the cryptosystems, and may safely skip over the proof summaries.
L148@P5: The survey is organized as follows:
L149@P5: • Chapter 2 recalls the necessary mathematical and cryptographic background.
L150@P5: • Chapter 3 gives a high-level conceptual overview of the seminal works in the area and their significance.
L151@P5: • Chapter 4 covers the modern foundations of the area, which have largely subsumed the earlier works.
L152@P5: Here we formally define the SIS and LWE problems and recall the theorems which say that these
L153@P5: problems are at least as hard to solve as certain worst-case lattice problems. We also cover their more
L154@P5: compact and efficient ring-based analogues, ring-SIS and ring-LWE.
L155@P5: • Chapter 5 describes a wide variety of essential lattice-based cryptographic constructions, ranging from
L156@P5: basic encryption and digital signatures to more powerful objects like identity-based encryption. These
L157@P5: schemes are presented within a unified framework, using just a handful of concepts and technical tools
L158@P5: that are developed throughout the chapter.
L159@P5: • Chapter 6 describes a few more advanced cryptographic constructions, with a focus on fully homomorphic encryption and attribute-based encryption.
L160@P5: • Chapter 7 concludes with a discussion of some important open questions in the area.
L161@P5: (comparatively simple) worst-case/average-case reductions, but only within a fixed group. Such a reduction gives us a distribution
L162@P5: over a group which is as hard as the worst case for the same group, but says nothing about whether the group itself is hard, or which
L163@P5: groups are hardest. Indeed, the complexity of these problems appears to vary quite widely depending on the type of group (e.g.,
L164@P5: multiplicative groups of integers modulo a prime or of other finite fields, elliptic curve groups, etc.).
L165@P5-6: 4While we have aimed to convey a wide variety of lattice-based cryptographic constructions and their
L166@P6: associated techniques, our coverage of such a large and fast-growing area is necessarily incomplete. For
L167@P6: one, we do not discuss cryptanalysis or concrete parameters (key sizes etc.) of lattice-based cryptosystems;
L168@P6: representative works on these topics include [GN08, MR09, GNR10, LP11, CN11, LN13]. We also do not
L169@P6: include any material on the recent seminal constructions of candidate multilinear maps [GGH13a, CLT13,
L170@P6: GGH15, CLT15] and their many exciting applications, such as general-purpose code obfuscation [GGH+13b,
L171@P6: SW14]. While all multilinear map constructions to date are related to lattices, their conjectured security relies
L172@P6: on new, ad-hoc problems that are much less well-understood than SIS/LWE. In particular, it is not known
L173@P6: whether any of the proposed constructions can be proved secure under worst-case hardness assumptions, and
L174@P6: some candidates have even been broken in certain ways (see, e.g., [CHL+15, HJ15, CL15, CGH+15]). Note
L175@P6: that early constructions of fully homomorphic encryption also relied on ad-hoc assumptions, but constructions
L176@P6: based on more standard assumptions like (ring-)LWE soon followed; the same may yet occur for multilinear
L177@P6: maps and the applications they enable.
L178@P6: 1.2 Other Resources
L179@P6: There are several other resources on modern lattice cryptography, or specialized subtopics thereof. (However,
L180@P6: due to the rapid development of the field over the past few years, these surveys are already a bit dated in
L181@P6: their coverage of advanced cryptographic constructions and associated techniques.) Some excellent options
L182@P6: include:
L183@P6: • The 2007 survey by Micciancio [Mic07] on cryptographic functions from worst-case complexity
L184@P6: assumptions, including ring-based functions;
L185@P6: • the 2009 survey by Micciancio and Regev [MR09] on lattice-based cryptographic constructions and
L186@P6: their cryptanalysis;
L187@P6: • the 2010 survey by Regev [Reg10] on the learning with errors (LWE) problem, its worst-case hardness,
L188@P6: and some early applications;
L189@P6: • the overviews of fully homomorphic encryption by Gentry [Gen10a] and Vaikuntanathan [Vai11];
L190@P6: • videos from the 2012 Bar-Ilan Winter School on Lattice Cryptography and Applications [Bar12];
L191@P6: • other surveys, books, and course notes [NS01, MG02, Reg04, Mic14] on computational aspects of
L192@P6: lattices, including cryptanalysis.

L31: ### 【17†The Direction of Updatable Encryption Does Matter】
L32: 
L33: Ryo Nishimaki, NTT Social Informatics Laboratories
L34: ##### Abstract
L35: We introduce a new definition for key updates, called backward-leak uni-directional key updates, in updatable encryption (UE). This notion is a variant of uni-directional key updates for UE. We show that existing secure UE schemes in the bi-directional key updates setting are not secure in the backward-leak uni-directional key updates setting. Thus, security in the backward-leak uni-directional key updates setting is strictly stronger than security in the bi-directional key updates setting.
L36: This result is in sharp contrast to the equivalence theorem by Jiang (Asiacrypt 2020), which says security in the bi-directional key updates setting is equivalent to security in the existing uni-directional key updates setting. We call the existing uni-directional key updates ``forward-leak uni-directional'' key updates to distinguish two types of uni-directional key updates in this paper.
L37: We also present a UE scheme that is secure in the backward-leak uni-directional key updates setting under the learning with errors assumption.
